summary: RADIANT generates, from a hand-authored requirement model, a concept model, a DSML (Emfatic/Ecore), a conforming EMF model (via generated EOL code) and a RoboChart behaviour model. Each phase uses AutoGen generate/check/refactor/trace agents plus a tool-driven check gate (Eclipse parser, EMF conformance, FDR model checking) with repair, and emits requirement-to-element trace links that drive change-impact analysis. On one autonomous-underwater-vehicle case study (10 runs x 3 LLMs) the pipeline beats one-shot single calls on syntactic validity (DeepSeek-V4 0.5 -> 1.0, Qwen3-max 0 -> 0.8), but semantic gains are model-dependent: Claude Sonnet 4.6 gets worse on DSML class F1. A six-person crossover reports 10-15x less time.

claims.claim: Multi-agent decomposition reliably improves syntactic validity of generated formal artefacts
claims.evidence: Table 2, §4.5: DSML syntax-valid 0.50 -> 1.00 (DeepSeek-V4, Fisher p=0.033) and 0.00 -> 0.80 (Qwen3-max, p=7.1e-4); Sonnet already 1.00. The single-agent baseline is one direct call per layer without the check gate, so the gain cannot be split between agent roles and parser/conformance feedback. 15 p-values uncorrected (acknowledged).

claims.claim: Executability improves where the model's code generation permits
claims.evidence: Conformant EOL models 0/10 -> 10/10 for DeepSeek-V4 (p=1.1e-5), 0/10 -> 4/10 for Qwen3-max (p=0.087, not significant), 0/10 under both configurations for Sonnet 4.6.

claims.claim: Executable element-level trace links with exact automated change-impact analysis
claims.evidence: §4.6: requirement-to-transition links match the 18-transition expert trace (F1 1.00, all models). Requirement-to-concept link micro-F1 is only 0.53-0.72, and behaviour-link resolvability is 0.73 for Sonnet. Change-impact F1 1.00 over 180 injected changes per model is measured only for behaviour requirements. The single-agent arm produces no trace, so there is no comparative baseline.

claims.claim: 10-15x reduction in development time with no accuracy cost
claims.evidence: Table 4, §4.7: manual 278-510 min vs automated 20-42 min, n=6 crossover. Automated participants reviewed one common DeepSeek-generated artefact, so automated accuracy is the pipeline's, not the person's. The model-to-text transformation is excluded from the totals, and the input requirement model was written to the pipeline's conventions.

claims.claim: The unmodified pipeline transfers to a second domain
claims.evidence: §4.8: SRanger (23 requirements, independently authored) passes every check gate including FDR; no expert reference, so no accuracy; one trace-resolution bug was found and fixed.

patterns.note: A trace agent emits requirement-to-artefact links in every phase; MALCOMj checks that link targets resolve, and requirement content hashes flag changed requirements for impact analysis. Behaviour links match the expert trace exactly (F1 1.00, 18 transitions), but requirement-to-concept links reach only 0.53-0.72 micro-F1. No comparison against post-hoc trace recovery or manual tracing; the single-agent arm emits no trace.

A tool-verified check gate (Eclipse parser, EMF Diagnostician, FDR) with a repair agent vs one-shot generation raises syntactic validity and executability significantly for 2 of 3 models (Table 2). The comparison is confounded with the multi-agent roles, since the baseline lacks both.

Semantic accuracy gain from multi-agent roles is model-dependent: positive for DeepSeek-V4, neutral for Qwen3-max, negative for Sonnet 4.6 (DSML class F1 0.92 -> 0.86, p=1.1e-3) because its check/refactor loop over-produces.

Structured requirement DSML with glossary, stakeholders and atomic requirements, and Concept/Instance marking conventions. Authors say the conventions improve generation 'from our experience', but this is not measured.
Generates machine-readable domain context (concept model, metamodel) from requirements and feeds it to later phases; not compared with phases lacking it.
FDR checks deadlock freedom and convergence with counterexample repair. Guards are abstracted to booleans for verifiability, so participants re-entered concrete guards by hand.
The requirement model is the single driver of all generation and the only manual phase; no comparison with a non-spec-driven workflow.

methodology.sample: One measured case study (AUV Last Response Engine; 18-transition behaviour) plus one unmeasured transfer (SRanger, 23 requirements); 10 repetitions per model x configuration; 6 participants for efficiency
methodology.baselines: Single agent (one direct call per layer, no check gate); manual modelling with the same MDE tools; no post-hoc traceability-recovery baseline; no other LLM-for-MDE system
methodology.variance: 10 runs per cell; Mann-Whitney U and Fisher exact tests; uncorrected across 15 comparisons (Bonferroni noted for the strongest)
methodology.ablations: Single vs multi only; agent roles and check gate not separated
methodology.contamination_controls: None; the LRE example comes from published RoboChart work (Foster et al. 2020), likely in training data; requirement model and expert reference authored by the authors
methodology.languages: Emfatic, EOL, RoboChart/CSP; Python (AutoGen) plus Java/Eclipse tooling

standards.artifacts: Full repository: requirement models, prompts and chain-of-thought assets, agent layer, MDE transformations, per-model configs, sweep results, evaluation harness

biases.detail: Authors wrote the requirement model and the expert reference used for scoring (acknowledged as residual construct risk).
The single-agent baseline lacks the parser/FDR check gate, so 'multi-agent decomposition' gets credit that may belong to tool feedback.
One measured case study; 6 participants in the efficiency study.
Efficiency compares people authoring from scratch against people reviewing a single pre-generated artefact; automated 'accuracy' is the pipeline's.
The AUV LRE state machine and requirements are from published papers.
No token, dollar or wall-clock generation cost per run.

coi.affiliations: Lancaster University; Tsinghua University; Harbin Institute of Technology; Dalian University of Technology; Southeast University; Loughborough University
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Three third-party LLMs compared neutrally; RADIANT/MALCOM is the authors' open-source tool
coi.detail: No vendor interest; own tool, with honest reporting of a model on which it underperforms.

verdict_reason: Repeated runs across three models, significance tests, fully released artefacts, and candid reporting that semantic gains are model-dependent and sometimes negative. Caveats: a single measured case study scored against the authors' own reference, a baseline that confounds agent roles with tool-verified repair, traceability accuracy that is exact only for simple state transitions, and an efficiency study that compares authoring against reviewing.
applicability: For the team's spec-to-code chain, the mechanism that transfers is traceability by construction. Every generation step emits requirement-to-artifact links, a deterministic tool checks that each link target exists, and requirement content hashes flag which artifacts a changed requirement affects. That maps onto a cheap qr-style check across 4 repos: requirement IDs in specs, links in generated Java and tests, hash-based staleness. Expect noisy links on domain concepts (content types, curricula, delivery contracts): requirement-to-concept links were only 0.53-0.72 F1, versus exact links for state transitions. The MDE/RoboChart stack itself does not transfer to Spring Boot services. RADIANT begins after the spec (the 'carefully engineered requirement model' is the one manual step), so it says nothing about pre-spec discovery beyond an anecdote that atomic requirements and a glossary help. Do not quote the 10-15x figure.

conflicts_with.detail: Copilot CLI assessing HIPAA-derived requirements against the iTrust Java codebase located requirement-satisfying code with F1 0.203, while RADIANT reports exact requirement-to-behaviour links. The difference is links generated by construction versus recovered post hoc by an agent; RADIANT's accuracy should not be read as evidence that agents can recover traceability on existing Java code.
